'''Franz Josef Gießibl''' (born 27 May 1962 in [[Amerang]]) is a German [[physicist]] and university professor at the [[University of Regensburg]].

== Life ==
Giessibl studied physics from 1982 to 1987 at the [[Technical University of Munich]] and at [[ETH Zurich|Eidgenössische Technischen Hochschule Zürich]]. He received a diploma in experimental physics in 1988 with Professor [[Gerhard Abstreiter]] and continued with a PhD in physics with Nobel Laureate [[Gerd Binnig]] at the IBM Physics Group Munich on [[atomic force microscopy]]. After submitting his PhD thesis in the end of 1991, he continued for 6 months as a Postdoctoral Fellow at the IBM Physics Group Munich and moved to Silicon Valley to join Park Scientific Instruments, Inc as a senior scientist and later director of vacuum products from mid 1992 until the end of 1994. He joined the Munich office of [[management consulting]] firm [[McKinsey & Company]] from 1995 to 1996 as a senior associate. During that time, he invented the {{Proper name|[[Non-contact atomic force microscopy|qPlus sensor]]}},<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.qplussensor.com|title=Website qPlus sensor}}</ref> a new probe for atomic force microscopy and continued experimental and theoretical work on the force microscope at the chair of Professor [[Jochen Mannhart]] at [[University of Augsburg]] where he received a [[habilitation]] in 2001.

In 2005, he obtained offers for a chair at the [[University of Bristol]] (England) and [[University of Regensburg]] (Germany).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uni-regensburg.de/physik/forschen/ag/franz-giessibl/team/prof-dr-franz-j-giessibl|title=CV Prof. Dr. Franz J. Gießibl – Universität Regensburg|website=www.uni-regensburg.de}}</ref> In 2006, he joined the faculty at the Department of Physics at the [[University of Regensburg]] in Germany.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uni-regensburg.de/physik/forschen/ag/franz-giessibl|title=Lehrstuhl Prof. Dr. Franz J. Gießibl – Universität Regensburg|website=www.uni-regensburg.de}}</ref> From about 2005, he collaborated with the scanning tunneling microscopy groups of [[IBM Almaden Research Center]] ([https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1150288 Science 2008)] and [[IBM Zurich Research Laboratory]] studying single-electron charges on single gold atoms [https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1172273 ''(Science 2009).''] and from about 2010 with [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-22886-7 ''(Nature Comm. 2021).''] to help to establish combined [[scanning tunneling microscopy]] and [[atomic force microscopy]] at ultralow temperatures. He was a visiting fellow at the center for nanoscience and technology (CNST) of the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] and a visiting professor at [[University of Maryland, College Park]] from fall 2015 to spring 2016 and at [[National University of Singapore]] with several research visits 2023 to 2025 [https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-08296-x  ''(Nature 2025).'']. He serves as a parttime research professor at [[Kanazawa University]].  <ref>{{cite news|url=https://ltphys.w3.kanazawa-u.ac.jp/qPlus_workshop2026/|title=The International Workshop on AFM/STM Using qPlus Sensors and Related Techniques – qPlus workshop 2026|last=pop|date=19 September 2026}}</ref>

Some of Giessibl's experimental and simulated images inspired the offset print editions ''Erster Blick'' (2000) and ''Graphit'' (2004) by visual artist [[Gerhard Richter]].<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1162/leon.2008.41.5.484| title = Nanotech, Blur and Tragedy in Recent Artworks by Gerhard Richter| journal = Leonardo| volume = 41| issue = 5| pages = 484–492| year = 2008| last1 = Nielsen | first1 = K. H. | s2cid = 57561154}}</ref><ref name="f923">{{cite book | last1=Giessibl | first1=Franz J. | last2=Richter | first2=Gerhard | title=Erster Blick in das Innere eines Atoms – Begegnungen mit Gerhard Richter zwischen Kunst und Wissenschaft | publisher=Verlag der Buchhandlung Walther und Franz König | publication-place=Köln | date=2022 | isbn=978-3-7533-0174-7 | oclc=1336840173 | url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/1336840173 | language=de | access-date=27 August 2026 | page=}}</ref> 

Franz Giessibl is married and has two sons.<ref>[https://www.uni-regensburg.de/fileadmin/sub-websites/physik/user_upload/AG/fgiessibl/PDF/Curriculum_Vitae_20230124_CV_e_Giessibl.pdf Uni Regensburg Giessibl CV]</ref>

== Scientific contributions ==
Giessibl established atomic force microscopy as a [[surface science]] tool with atomic resolution,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Giessibl | first1 = F. J. | s2cid = 20978364 | year = 1995 | title = Atomic resolution of the Silicon (111)-(7x7) surface by atomic force microscopy. | journal = Science | volume = 267 | issue = 5194| pages = 68–71 | doi=10.1126/science.267.5194.68 | pmid = 17840059 | bibcode=1995Sci...267...68G| url = https://epub.uni-regensburg.de/33828/1/Atomic%20Resolution%20of%20the%20Silicon%20%28111%29-%287x7%29%20Surface%20by.pdf }}</ref> launching the field of [[Non-contact atomic force microscopy]]. ScholarGPS lists him among the six most highly ranked scholars in atomic force microscopy (lifetime) and among the 14 most highly ranked scholars in microscopy (lifetime).<ref name="b792">{{cite web | title=Scholar Profiles and Rankings | website=ScholarGPS | url=https://scholargps.com/scholars/29978332049213/franz-j-giessibl | access-date=26 April 2026}}</ref> Together with his team, he even obtained subatomic spatial resolution ({{cite journal | last1=Giessibl | first1=Franz J. | last2=Hembacher | first2=S. | last3=Bielefeldt | first3=H. | last4=Mannhart | first4=J. | title=Subatomic Features on the Silicon (111)-(7×7) Surface Observed by Atomic Force Microscopy | journal=Science | volume=289 | issue=5478 | date=21 July 2000 | issn=0036-8075 | doi=10.1126/science.289.5478.422 | pages=422–425 | url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.289.5478.422 | access-date=27 August 2026| url-access=subscription }}),<ref>{{cite of atomic force microscopy. 
Giessibl is the inventor of the  [[Non-contact atomic force microscopy|qPlus sensor]],<ref>F. J. Giessibl: ''Device for noncontact intermittent contact scanning of a surface and a process therefore.'' US Patent 6240771</ref><ref>F. J. Giessibl: ''Sensor for noncontact profiling of a surface.'' US Patent 8393009</ref> a sensor for [[Non-contact atomic force microscopy]] that relies on a quartz cantilever. His invention has enabled atomic force microscopy to obtain subatomic spatial resolution on individual atoms and submolecular resolution on organic molecules. Today, the qPlus sensor is used in more than 500 commercial and homebuilt atomic force microscopes around the world.

* 1992: Built the first low-temperature force microscope for ultrahigh vacuum with [[Gerd Binnig]] (PhD adviser) and [[Christoph Gerber]]
** {{cite journal | last1=Giessibl | first1=F. J. | last2=Gerber | first2=Ch. | last3=Binnig | first3=G. | title=A low-temperature atomic force/scanning tunneling microscope for ultrahigh vacuum | journal=Journal of Vacuum Science & Technology B: Microelectronics and Nanometer Structures Processing, Measurement, and Phenomena | volume=9 | issue=2 | date=1 March 1991 | issn=1071-1023 | doi=10.1116/1.585441 | pages=984–988 | bibcode=1991JVSTB...9..984G | url=https://pubs.aip.org/jvb/article/9/2/984/1030490/A-low-temperature-atomic-force-scanning-tunneling | access-date=27 August 2026| url-access=subscription }}
* and obtained atomic resolution on KBr with it
** {{cite journal | last1=Giessibl | first1=F.J. | last2=Binnig | first2=G. | title=Investigation of the (001) cleavage plane of potassium bromide with an atomic force microscope at 4.2 K in ultra-high vacuum | journal=Ultramicroscopy | volume=42–44 | date=1992 | doi=10.1016/0304-3991(92)90280-W | pages=281–289 | url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/030439919290280W | access-date=27 August 2026| url-access=subscription }}. KBr has a very low reactivity, yet major challenges such as jump-to-contact of AFM tip and sample had to be overcome to obtain atomic resolution.
